<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

</document>
response:
# Review: Achterberg et al., "Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis"

**Bottom line:** this is a careful synthesis, and its main conclusions are sound:
- a real but modest gain in output per hour, about 8–10% in the better-designed studies;
- no meaningful loss of output per worker in discretionary work;
- a clear loss of output per worker in coverage-bound work;
- support for neither the "entirely an artifact" claim nor the "sector-general" claim.

It also settles the disagreement between the three earlier papers sensibly. The weaknesses are:
- one overreaching claim, that novelty effects "can be set aside";
- a publication-bias interpretation that ignores an obvious confound;
- "convergence" across subgroups that isn't independent confirmation;
- some ambiguity about how Varden and Halden were coded and which Halden figures were used;
- no formal risk-of-bias assessment.

## What checks out

**Counts are internally consistent.**
- 9 + 14 = 23 by design, 8 + 15 by hours measure, 12 + 11 by output measure, 13 + 7 + 3 by work type.
- The overlap statements imply 3 controlled studies used scheduled hours and 2 used manager-reported output. That is consistent with the subgroup counts.

**Confidence intervals are symmetric on the log scale, as they should be for log ratios.**
- Overall: ln(1.081) = 0.078 and ln(1.190) = 0.174, with midpoint 0.126 = ln(1.134) ✓.
- The prediction interval (−4% to +34%) is centred on the same point ✓.
- The bias-adjusted, controlled, duration, coverage-bound and mixed intervals all centre correctly as well.

**The implied hours reductions are plausible.** Dividing the per-worker change by the per-hour change gives the implied fall in hours for each subgroup:

| Subgroup | Implied hours reduction |
|---|---|
| All studies | ≈ 13% |
| Actual hours | ≈ 11% |
| Scheduled hours | ≈ 15% |
| Coverage-bound | ≈ 14% |

The smaller implied reduction in the actual-hours studies fits Varden's and Varga & Holm's findings that actual hours fall less than scheduled hours.

**The coverage-bound result matches Varden.** The pooled −8.9% per worker and +6.2% per hour are close to Varden's counter stratum (−11.4% and +6.7%).

---

## 1. The duration conclusion is overstated

"Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" is the weakest claim in the paper, and it appears in the Abstract.

- **The interval is too wide to rule out decay.** The four long-follow-up studies give +14.0% (6.2 to 22.4). That is compatible with a drop to around 6%, which is well within what a novelty effect could produce.
- **The comparison group is wrong.** The four long studies should be compared with studies of the *same design* followed for shorter periods, not with the overall estimate. If they are mostly uncontrolled scheduled-hours studies, their natural reference is +16.6–18.7%, and 14.0% would then be *lower*.
- **This compares studies, not trajectories.** Decay is a pattern within a study over time. The right test uses studies reporting output at several time points, comparing early with late effects within each study. The median follow-up is 6 months, so some studies should have this data.
- **Survivorship.** Schemes that fail tend to stop early, so long follow-ups come disproportionately from schemes that worked.
- **The Limitations section already admits the problem.** It says "Most studies are short", which sits awkwardly with dismissing novelty in the Abstract.

**Suggested wording:** "The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months show gains of similar size, but they are too few and too heterogeneous to rule out partial decay."

## 2. The small-study bias may mostly reflect study design

The asymmetric funnel plot is read as evidence that favourable results are more likely to be published. That may be part of it, but there is a confound. The small studies are likely to be the uncontrolled pilots using scheduled hours and manager reports, and those features are already known to produce larger estimates. Asymmetry can arise from this heterogeneity alone.

- Trim-and-fill is known to perform poorly when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%).
- **Fix:** run Egger's test or PET-PEESE *with the moderators in the model*, or within the controlled subgroup. If the asymmetry disappears once design is controlled for, the bias-adjusted 9.1% is mostly another version of the design correction, not a separate one.

## 3. The "convergence" isn't independent confirmation

The Discussion says controlled studies, actual-hours studies, record-based studies and the bias-adjusted estimate "converge on roughly 8 to 10%". But these subgroups largely contain the same studies:
- 6 of the 8 actual-hours studies are controlled;
- 7 of the 12 record-based studies are controlled.

So the agreement mostly reflects the same handful of controlled studies counted several times. Presenting it as several independent lines of evidence overstates the case.

**Fix:** the honest single estimate is the controlled studies, ideally with actual hours and records together. Report that intersection as a separate cell, even though k will be small.

## 4. How Varden and Halden were coded is unclear

These two studies matter most to the debate, so the paper should state exactly how they entered the analysis.

- **Varden** has a discretionary stratum and a coverage-bound stratum, but each study has only one work-type code (13 + 7 + 3 = 23).
  - If Varden was coded "mixed", its clean stratum results are lost.
  - If its strata were entered separately, there are 24 effect sizes and the counts need correcting.
- **Halden** covers six sectors, including retail.
  - The "mixed" category has only three studies, and two of them are manufacturing.
  - So Halden and Varden cannot both be coded "mixed". Which was coded how?
- **Which Halden figures were used?** The rule "where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours" leaves a question open. Did the review use Halden's original 23.4% (scheduled hours, manager reports) or Varga & Holm's corrected subset? Using both would double-count. Either choice needs justifying, and a sensitivity analysis would help.

## 5. No formal risk-of-bias assessment

The review analyses design features as moderators, but it doesn't appear to use a standard risk-of-bias tool such as RoB 2 or ROBINS-I, or to rate certainty of evidence with GRADE. Several issues raised across these papers fall outside the three moderators:
- **Attrition and withdrawal.** Halden's withdrawals took place after the schedule began.
- **Evaluator conflicts.** Examples are managers acting as sponsors, or pilots run or reported by advocacy organisations.
- **Selective reporting of outcomes.**

These should be assessed and used in a sensitivity analysis. An attrition moderator is especially relevant given the Halden findings.

## 6. Inference with few studies

- Subgroups of k = 3–9 with substantial heterogeneity make standard random-effects intervals too narrow. The paper should apply the Hartung–Knapp adjustment, at least for the controlled, actual-hours and coverage-bound subgroups.
- Report prediction intervals for the key subgroups, not just the overall estimate. The controlled-discretionary prediction interval is the figure most useful to an employer.
- A meta-regression with three correlated moderators on 23 studies is at risk of overfitting. The 58% of variance explained should be treated as descriptive, not as a firm estimate. The Limitations section partly concedes this.

## 7. The secondary outcomes need the same scrutiny

- **"Sick leave fell in all 14 studies"** is vote-counting, and it repeats the measurement problem raised for both Halden and Varden. If staff work fewer days, there are fewer days on which absence can be recorded. Report how many studies measured sick leave per scheduled day, and pool those separately.
- **Selective reporting.** Studies may be more likely to report sick leave and turnover when they fell. "All 14" and "all 9" are therefore weaker evidence than they look.
- **Turnover** has no pooled estimate.

## 8. Smaller points

- **The mechanism correlation is uninformative, not negative.** r = 0.18 across 11 studies has a 95% interval of roughly −0.47 to 0.70. It is also an ecological correlation between studies, which can't test whether individual workers' fatigue drives their productivity. Say so explicitly so readers don't treat it as evidence against fatigue.
- **The coverage-bound per-hour gain probably reflects utilisation.** With fewer staff on duty, each one spends less time idle between customers, as discussed in my Varden review. "Real" is accurate arithmetically, but readers may take it to mean staff working more effectively.
- **The search is small.** 412 records screened is a small search for this topic. Much of the pilot evidence is grey literature from advocacy organisations, so list the sources searched and consider sponsor type as a moderator.
- **The excluded "mixed" category matters.** Most real organisations are mixed, so the paper's own Limitations point about forcing work into binary categories deserves more weight in the Discussion.

---

## Where the four papers leave the question

Taken together, the evidence now supports a fairly clear picture:

| Question | Best current answer | Main sources |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | ~8–12%, real | Varden case-processing (+12.5%), Varga & Holm corrected (+10.8%), meta-analysis controlled-discretionary (+9.6%) |
| Per-worker output, discretionary | Roughly maintained; a loss of a few percent not ruled out | Varden (−2.1%), meta-analysis (−2.7%) |
| Per-worker output, coverage-bound | Falls ~9–11%, and service gets worse | Varden counter, meta-analysis (I² = 22%) |
| Headline gains above 20% | Mostly an artifact of scheduled-hours denominators and manager reports | All three critical papers |
| Durability beyond about a year | **Open** | Too little data; Varden 24-month follow-up pending |
| Mechanism (rest vs. removing low-value time) | **Open** | Varden's registered meetings test pending |

The meta-analysis is right to reject both extremes. Its one significant overreach is treating the durability question as closed.
